examples.ko: 우리 회사는 특허를 열 개 보유해요.
examples.en: Our company holds ten patents.

examples.ko: 그 선수는 세계 기록을 보유하고 있어요.
examples.en: That athlete holds a world record.
The money the bank holds has dropped a lot.

examples.ko: 이 병원은 내년에 새 장비를 보유할 거예요.
examples.en: This hospital will have new equipment next year.

examples.ko: 예전에는 이 나라가 큰 군대를 보유했어요.
examples.en: This country used to maintain a large army.

examples.ko: 집을 두 채 보유해서 세금이 많아요.
examples.en: I own two houses, so my taxes are high.

explain: '가지다'는 아무 물건에나 쓰지만, '보유하다'는 회사·나라·단체가 기록, 재산, 기술 같은 것을 가지고 있을 때 써요. 뉴스와 서류에서 자주 보여요. 보통 '보유하고 있다'로 말해요.
explain_en: '가지다' works for any object, but '보유하다' is used when a company, country, or group holds records, assets, or technology. It shows up in news and documents. It is usually said as '보유하고 있다'.

examples.en: My application was approved yesterday.
The new plan was approved at the meeting.
I will contact you right away when the loan is approved.

examples.ko: 승인된 사람만 이 문으로 들어갈 수 있어요.
examples.en: Only approved people can enter through this door.
I am upset because my leave was not approved.
I got a text saying the payment was approved.

explain: '승인되다'는 허락하는 사람이 따로 있을 때 써요. 대출·휴가·결제처럼 윗사람이나 기관이 결정하는 일에 어울려요. 허락하는 쪽에서는 '승인하다'를 써요. '허락되다'는 일상 말이고, '승인되다'는 서류와 앱 알림에서 더 자주 보여요.
explain_en: '승인되다' fits things decided by someone with authority, such as loans, leave, or payments. The person or body giving permission uses '승인하다'. '허락되다' is more everyday, while '승인되다' appears more in documents and app notifications.

examples.en: My team leader approved my leave.
The company will approve the new budget.
The card company approved the payment.

examples.ko: 부모님이 승인하면 학생이 앱을 쓸 수 있어요.
examples.en: If a parent approves, the student can use the app.
The person who approves it is not at their desk now.

examples.ko: 위원회가 승인한 약만 팔 수 있어요.
examples.en: Only medicine that the committee approved can be sold.

explain: '허락하다'는 누구나 쓰는 말이고, '승인하다'는 서류·예산·결제처럼 정해진 절차를 거쳐 허락할 때 써요. 받는 쪽은 '승인되다'를 써요. 반대말은 '거부하다'예요.
explain_en: '허락하다' is for any permission, while '승인하다' is for approval through a set procedure, such as documents, budgets, or payments. The receiving side uses '승인되다'. The opposite is '거부하다'.

en: be manufactured; be made (in a factory)

examples.en: This bag was manufactured in Italy.
This medicine is made in a clean factory.
Cosmetics made in Korea are very popular.
I watched the manufacturing process in a video.

examples.ko: 이 제품은 내년부터 베트남에서도 제조될 거예요.
examples.en: This product will also be manufactured in Vietnam from next year.
It is made at the factory and delivered right away.

explain: '만들어지다'는 일상 말이고, '제조되다'는 공장에서 물건이 만들어질 때 써요. 상품 포장에 '한국에서 제조'라고 쓴 것을 본 적이 있을 거예요. '제조사'(만드는 회사), '제조일'(만든 날)처럼 같이 보이는 말도 알아 두세요.
explain_en: '만들어지다' is everyday, while '제조되다' is for goods made in a factory. You may have seen '한국에서 제조' on packaging. Related words you will see are '제조사' (the maker) and '제조일' (the production date).

examples.en: The thief was arrested last night.
That person was arrested by the police.
They say the arrested man admitted the facts.
If the criminal is arrested, it will be on the news.
He ended up being arrested while running away.
The arrest scene was caught on video.

explain: '잡히다'는 일상에서 쓰고, '체포되다'는 경찰이 법에 따라 잡았을 때 써요. 그래서 뉴스에서 자주 들어요. '경찰에게 체포되다'처럼 '에게'를 써요. 잡은 경찰 쪽 말은 '체포하다'예요.
explain_en: '잡히다' is everyday, while '체포되다' is for when the police catch someone under the law, so you hear it often in the news. It takes '에게', as in '경찰에게 체포되다'. The police side uses '체포하다'.

examples.en: The police arrested the thief.

examples.ko: 경찰은 그 남자를 곧 체포할 거예요.
examples.en: The police will arrest that man soon.
I watched a movie about arresting a criminal.
They took the arrested person to the police station.

examples.ko: 경찰이 길에서 그 사람을 체포하고 이름을 물었어요.
examples.en: The police arrested him on the street and asked his name.

examples.ko: 아직 체포하지 못해서 계속 찾고 있어요.
examples.en: They have not been able to arrest him yet, so they keep looking.

explain: '잡다'는 누구나 쓰지만 '체포하다'는 경찰이나 수사 기관이 할 때만 써요. 친구를 붙잡았을 때는 쓰지 않아요. 뉴스에서는 '검거하다'도 비슷하게 쓰는데, 경찰 쪽에서 쓰는 말이에요.
explain_en: Anyone can use '잡다', but '체포하다' is only for police or investigators. You would not use it when you grab a friend. In the news, '검거하다' is used similarly, but it is the police's own word.

en: be finalized; be confirmed; be settled

examples.en: The schedule has not been finalized yet.
Our team's departure date has been confirmed.
I will tell you as soon as your acceptance is confirmed.
Please tell people only the finalized plan.
The day the exam results are finalized is Friday.

examples.ko: 가격이 확정돼서 포스터를 만들 수 있어요.
examples.en: The price is settled, so we can make the poster.

explain: '정해지다'는 일상에서 아무 때나 쓰지만, '확정되다'는 바뀔 수 있던 일이 마지막으로 정해졌을 때 써요. 일정·가격·합격 같은 말과 잘 어울려요. 아직 안 정해졌을 때는 '미정'이라고 해요.
explain_en: '정해지다' is the everyday word, while '확정되다' is for something that could still change and has now been settled for good. It pairs well with schedules, prices, and acceptances. When something is not yet decided, people say '미정'.

examples.en: He was hired by a small restaurant.
I was hired by a new company last month.
The people who were hired start work tomorrow.
When you are hired as an employee, you sign a contract.
Ten people in total will be hired.
I am hired only three days a week.

explain: '취직하다'는 내가 일자리를 얻었다는 느낌이고, '고용되다'는 회사가 나를 쓰기로 했다는 쪽에서 말해요. 보통 '식당에 고용되다'처럼 '에'를 써요. 회사 쪽은 '고용하다'예요.
explain_en: '취직하다' says that I got a job, while '고용되다' describes it from the side of the company choosing to use me. It usually takes '에', as in '식당에 고용되다'. The company side uses '고용하다'.

examples.en: The owner hired three employees.
Our shop does not hire students.
I do not have the money to hire anyone yet.
The newly hired employee is very kind.
It can be hard for the side that hires, too.
We are short-handed, so I want to hire a part-timer.

explain: '뽑다'는 지원자 중에서 고르는 것이고, '고용하다'는 뽑은 뒤 일하게 하는 것까지 말해요. 일하는 사람 쪽에서는 '고용되다'라고 해요. 반대말은 '해고하다'예요.
explain_en: '뽑다' is choosing from applicants, while '고용하다' includes having the person work afterward. The worker's side uses '고용되다'. The opposite is '해고하다'.

en: be carried out; be executed; (a program) run

examples.en: The plan will be carried out next week.
The program ran as soon as the app opened.
This command runs when you press the button.
Not a single plan was carried out.
Do not turn off the screen while it is running.
I only noticed the problem after it was carried out.

explain: 컴퓨터에서 프로그램이 돌아갈 때도, 계획이나 정책이 실제로 시작될 때도 써요. 컴퓨터에서는 내가 프로그램을 돌리는 쪽이 '실행하다', 프로그램이 돌아가는 상태가 '실행되다'예요. '실천하다'는 내가 마음먹은 일을 직접 하는 것이라 사람에게 써요.
explain_en: It is used both when a program runs on a computer and when a plan or policy is actually put into action. On a computer, '실행하다' is the side where I start the program, and '실행되다' is the state of it running. '실천하다' is for a person carrying out what they resolved to do.

en: be stagnant; be stalled; (traffic) be congested

examples.en: The roads get congested at rush hour.

examples.ko: 우리 회사의 성장이 몇 년째 정체되었어요.
examples.en: Our company's growth has been stagnant for years.
The traffic jam lasted so long that I was very late.
Exports have been stagnant for months, so I am worried.
I want to change the stagnant mood.
Cars are backed up because of the snow.

explain: 길이 막힐 때는 '막히다'가 더 일상적이고, '정체되다'는 뉴스의 교통 정보에서 자주 나와요. 일이나 경제가 앞으로 나아가지 않을 때도 써요. 반대로 빠르게 나아갈 때는 '성장하다', '발전하다'를 써요.
explain_en: For roads, '막히다' is more everyday, and '정체되다' appears often in news traffic reports. It also describes work or the economy that is not moving forward. When things move ahead quickly, you say '성장하다' or '발전하다'.

en: be created; be formed; be built (park, fund, atmosphere)

examples.en: A new plaza was built next to the park.
A safe road was created in front of the school.

examples.ko: 조성된 기금은 도서관을 짓는 데 쓸 거예요.
examples.en: The fund that was raised will be used to build a library.

examples.ko: 산 아래에 마을이 조성되는 모습을 봤어요.
examples.en: I watched a village being built at the foot of the mountain.
Once the mood is set, it is easy to talk.
A walking path will be built around the lake.

explain: '만들어지다'보다 딱딱해서 공원·단지·기금·분위기처럼 크고 계획된 것에 써요. 개인 물건에는 잘 안 써요. '분위기가 조성되다', '기금이 조성되다'처럼 짝이 되는 말이 거의 정해져 있어요. 만드는 쪽은 '조성하다'예요.
explain_en: It is stiffer than '만들어지다' and is used for large, planned things such as parks, complexes, funds, and atmospheres. It is rarely used for personal items. It has set partners like '분위기가 조성되다' and '기금이 조성되다'. The side that creates uses '조성하다'.

examples.en: The city hall built a park by the river.
The teacher created a comfortable atmosphere for us.

examples.ko: 친구들과 돈을 모아 기금을 조성할 거예요.
examples.en: We will pool our money and set up a fund.
The people who created the forest received an award.

examples.ko: 마을 정원을 조성하는 데 오 년이 걸렸어요.
examples.en: It took five years to create the village garden.

examples.ko: 학생들이 공부하기 좋은 환경을 조성하고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to create a good environment for students to study.

explain: '만들다'는 아무 때나 쓰지만 '조성하다'는 공원·기금·분위기·환경처럼 큰 대상에 써요. 작은 물건이나 음식에는 쓰지 않아요. '분위기를 조성하다', '환경을 조성하다'가 가장 많이 쓰는 짝이에요.
explain_en: '만들다' works anywhere, but '조성하다' is for large targets such as parks, funds, atmospheres, and environments. It is not used for small objects or food. '분위기를 조성하다' and '환경을 조성하다' are the most common pairings.

examples.ko: 그 나라는 옛날에 이 섬을 지배했어요.
examples.en: That country ruled this island long ago.
Fear is controlling my mind.
A big company dominates the market.
There were those who ruled and those who were ruled.
Do not let your emotions control you.
It was a day when that team dominated the game.

explain: 나라나 사람이 다른 사람을 힘으로 움직일 때뿐 아니라, 감정이나 분위기가 사람을 움직일 때도 써요. 당하는 쪽은 '지배받다'라고 해요. '다스리다'는 나라를 이끈다는 좋은 느낌도 있지만, '지배하다'는 힘으로 누른다는 느낌이 강해요.
explain_en: It describes a country or person controlling others by force, and also feelings or moods controlling a person. The side being ruled uses '지배받다'. '다스리다' can sound positive, like governing well, while '지배하다' feels like pressing down by force.

examples.en: The law was revised this year.
The textbook was newly revised.
Be sure to read the revised rules.
I will send a text when the price list is revised.
The exam system is being revised.
The terms were revised, so I got a notification.

explain: '개정'은 법·규칙·책의 내용을 고치는 것이에요. 있는 법을 고칠 때는 '개정', 없던 법을 새로 만들 때는 '제정'이에요. 서점에서 보이는 '개정판'은 고쳐서 다시 낸 책이에요. 소리가 비슷한 '개선'(더 좋게 고침)과 헷갈리지 마세요.
explain_en: '개정' is changing the content of laws, rules, or books. Changing an existing law is '개정', while making a new one is '제정'. In bookstores, '개정판' is a revised edition. Do not confuse it with the similar-sounding '개선' (improvement).

examples.en: The government revised the law.
The publisher will revise the book.
The school decided to revise its rules.
Revising takes a long time.
We posted the revised content on the website.

examples.ko: 회사가 이용 약관을 개정하고 사용자에게 알렸어요.
examples.en: The company revised its terms of use and notified users.

explain: '고치다'는 틀린 것도 낡은 물건도 고치지만, '개정하다'는 법·규칙·약관 같은 문서의 내용을 공식적으로 바꿀 때만 써요. 하는 쪽은 정부나 회사 같은 곳이에요. 일상 대화에서 '내 계획을 개정했어요'라고는 하지 않아요.
explain_en: '고치다' fixes mistakes and old things, but '개정하다' is only for officially changing documents such as laws, rules, or terms. The one doing it is a body like a government or company. In daily talk you would not say '내 계획을 개정했어요'.

en: be held in a collection; be kept (in a museum or library)

examples.en: That painting is kept in the national museum.
This book was added to the university library's collection.
The works in the collection number over three thousand.
I heard that an old map is held in the collection.
Experts examine works first before they enter the collection.

examples.ko: 이 유물은 내년부터 새 건물에 소장될 거예요.
examples.en: This relic will be housed in the new building from next year.

explain: '소장'은 박물관·도서관·개인이 귀한 것을 보관하는 것이에요. '보관되다'보다 귀한 작품이나 책에 어울려요. 물건을 모아 두는 쪽은 '소장하다'예요.
explain_en: '소장' means a museum, library, or individual keeping something valuable. It fits precious works and books more than '보관되다' does. The side that keeps the collection uses '소장하다'.

en: cut (cloth or paper to a pattern); judge or size up (someone) by your own standard

examples.en: I cut the fabric first and then sew.
The designer cut the cloth to size.
Do not judge people so carelessly.
Words that size others up hurt them.
This cloth is easy to cut.

examples.ko: 책 크기에 맞게 종이를 재단해서 쓰고 있어요.
examples.en: I cut paper to fit the book size and use it.

explain: 원래는 옷감이나 종이를 모양에 맞게 자르는 일이에요. 요즘은 '남을 재단하다'처럼 내 기준으로 사람을 함부로 판단한다는 뜻으로 더 자주 써요. 이때는 나쁜 느낌이라 '재단하지 마세요'처럼 충고할 때 많이 써요.

phrases.en: Do not judge others just by their looks.
phrases.nuance_ko: 내 기준에 맞춰 사람을 함부로 판단한다는 비판의 느낌이에요.
phrases.nuance_en: Criticizes judging a person carelessly by your own standard.

explain_en: Originally it means cutting cloth or paper to a shape. Today it is used more often as '남을 재단하다', meaning to judge people carelessly by your own standard. In that sense it feels negative and is often used in advice like '재단하지 마세요'.

en: take action; take steps; deal with

examples.en: If a problem comes up, please deal with it right away.
They say the company has already taken action.
I discussed with the team how to handle it.
If we do not act quickly, there will be big trouble.
It took less than a day to deal with it.
I will send you by email what we did about it.

explain: '조치'는 문제가 생겼을 때 해결하려고 하는 행동이에요. '조치하다'도 쓰지만 '필요한 조치를 취하다'처럼 '조치를 취하다'가 더 자주 들려요. 회사 공지나 고객센터 답변에서 자주 볼 수 있어요.
explain_en: '조치' is an action taken to solve a problem. '조치하다' is used, but '조치를 취하다', as in '필요한 조치를 취하다', is heard more often. You often see it in company notices and customer-service replies.

examples.en: I was selected as a representative player.

examples.ko: 열 명 중에서 두 명이 선발되었어요.
examples.en: Two out of ten were selected.
The selected students will meet next week.

examples.ko: 시험을 잘 보면 선발될 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you do well on the test, you can be selected.
They give a prize to the people who are selected.
I failed the test and was not selected.

explain: '뽑히다'는 일상에서 쓰는 말이고, '선발되다'는 대회·장학금·팀처럼 공식적인 선택에 써요. 뽑는 쪽은 '선발하다'예요. 일자리를 얻는 일은 '채용되다'가 더 자연스러워요.
explain_en: '뽑히다' is everyday, while '선발되다' is for official selection such as competitions, scholarships, and teams. The choosing side uses '선발하다'. For getting a job, '채용되다' is more natural.

examples.en: This event is limited to students.
The sale period is limited to this week.

examples.ko: 한정된 시간 안에 문제를 풀어야 해요.
examples.en: You have to solve the problems within a limited time.
The number of places is limited, so apply quickly.
It is an app whose range of use is limited.
It is a story that is not limited to one person.

explain: '한정되다'는 범위나 수가 정해져서 그 밖은 안 된다는 느낌이에요. '한정판'(수를 정해서 만든 물건), '한정 메뉴'처럼 가게에서도 자주 보여요. 비슷한 '제한되다'는 규칙으로 막는다는 느낌이 더 강해요.
explain_en: '한정되다' feels like the range or number is fixed and nothing outside it is allowed. You often see '한정판' (limited edition) and '한정 메뉴' in shops. The similar '제한되다' feels more like being blocked by a rule.

examples.en: The book was damaged because it got rained on.
The old painting was damaged by sunlight.
Please send a photo of the damaged part.

examples.ko: 상자가 손상되면 환불을 받을 수 있어요.
examples.en: If the box is damaged, you can get a refund.
My hair was damaged and split, so I went to the salon.

examples.ko: 손상되는 일이 없도록 포장을 두껍게 했어요.
examples.en: I wrapped it thickly so it would not get damaged.

explain: '망가지다'는 물건이 못 쓰게 됐을 때 일상에서 쓰고, '손상되다'는 조금 다치거나 상한 것에도 써요. 물건뿐 아니라 '명예가 손상되다', '이미지가 손상되다'처럼 눈에 안 보이는 것에도 써요. 기계가 안 움직일 때는 '고장 나다'를 써요.
explain_en: '망가지다' is the everyday word for something that can no longer be used, while '손상되다' also covers slight damage. It applies to things you cannot see too, as in '명예가 손상되다' and '이미지가 손상되다'. For a machine that does not work, use '고장 나다'.

examples.en: They say the famous writer passed away last night.
He passed away quietly in the hospital.
I wrote down the date he passed away in the book.
Before passing away, he left a letter for his family.

examples.ko: 삼 년 전에 운명한 시인의 시를 읽었어요.
examples.en: I read a poem by a poet who passed away three years ago.
Everyone was shocked at the news that he had passed away.

explain: '죽다'보다 아주 격식 있는 말이에요. 주로 신문 기사나 장례식 같은 자리에서 써요. 높일 때는 '돌아가시다'가 훨씬 더 일반적이니 일상에서는 '돌아가시다'를 쓰세요. 소리가 같은 '운명'(타고난 앞날)과 헷갈리지 마세요.
explain_en: This is a very formal word for dying, mainly in newspaper articles and funeral settings. In daily life, '돌아가시다' is far more common when showing respect, so use that. Do not confuse it with the same-sounding '운명' (fate).

examples.en: In the novel, a rich man is murdered.
The man was murdered in front of his house.
The family of the murdered person is grieving.
The criminal fled before the victim was murdered.
He was found two days after being murdered.
The police saved a person who was nearly murdered.

explain: '죽임을 당하다'와 같은 뜻이지만 뉴스·수사 기사에서는 '살해되다'를 써요. 사고나 병으로 죽은 경우에는 쓰지 않고, 누군가가 일부러 죽였을 때만 써요. 죽인 쪽 말은 '살해하다'예요.
explain_en: It means the same as '죽임을 당하다', but news and investigation reports use '살해되다'. It is not used for deaths by accident or illness, only when someone killed on purpose. The killer's side uses '살해하다'.

examples.en: The criminal murdered the victim.

examples.ko: 소설에서 그가 왜 친구를 살해했는지 알 수 있어요.
examples.en: In the novel, you can learn why he killed his friend.
Stories about murder are scary.

examples.ko: 경찰은 그를 살해한 사람을 찾고 있어요.
examples.en: The police are looking for the person who killed him.
The claim that he tried to murder someone was false.
There was no evidence that he committed the murder.

explain: '죽이다'보다 훨씬 딱딱해서 뉴스·법원·소설에서 써요. 일상 대화에서는 '죽이다'를 쓰고, 이 말은 쓰지 않는 편이에요. 사람이 아닌 동물에게는 보통 쓰지 않아요.
explain_en: It is much stiffer than '죽이다' and appears in news, courts, and novels. In everyday talk people say '죽이다' and rarely use this word. It is usually not used for animals.

examples.en: I know it is a bother, but please check just once.
Preparing to move is more of a hassle than you think.
Guiding each guest one by one was laborious.
If it is too much trouble, I will do it for you.

examples.ko: 수고롭지 않다면 문 좀 열어 주실래요?
examples.en: If it is no trouble, could you open the door?
Getting up at dawn every day is a burden.

explain: '수고롭다'는 일이 번거롭고 애써야 해서 힘들 때 써요. 부탁할 때 '수고로우시겠지만'을 앞에 붙이면 정중해요. ㅂ 불규칙이라 '수고로워요', '수고로운'이 돼요. 일을 마친 사람에게 하는 인사 '수고했어요'와는 쓰임이 달라요.
explain_en: '수고롭다' describes something that takes bothersome effort. Putting '수고로우시겠지만' before a request makes it polite. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, giving '수고로워요' and '수고로운'. It is used differently from the greeting '수고했어요' said to someone who finished work.

examples.en: The sudden news threw people into confusion.
That rumor is throwing the village into disorder.
Did you do it on purpose to confuse me?
If you keep changing what you say, you confuse the students.
Please do not do things that cause confusion.

examples.ko: 새 규칙이 손님들을 혼란시킨 것 같아요.
examples.en: It seems the new rule confused the customers.

explain: '혼란시키다'는 누가 일부러든 아니든 다른 사람을 헷갈리게 하고 질서를 흐트러뜨릴 때 써요. 내가 헷갈릴 때는 '혼란스럽다'가 훨씬 자연스러워요. 일상에서는 '헷갈리게 하다'를 더 많이 말해요.
explain_en: '혼란시키다' is used when something, on purpose or not, makes others confused and upsets order. When I am the confused one, '혼란스럽다' is much more natural. In daily talk, '헷갈리게 하다' is more common.
